claims.text: The starting coating has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a dominant FCC matrix and discretely distributed BCC precipitates or regions.
Enhanced creep resistance arises from synergy between a load-bearing BCC phase and FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries impede dislocation glide.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries impede dislocation climb.
The BCC regions are stiffer than the surrounding FCC matrix and consequently bear load.
The combined load-bearing and interphase-barrier effects delay the onset and progression of plastic deformation during continuous loading.
Delaying dislocation-mediated plastic deformation retards creep.
BCC volume fraction or FCC/BCC interface quality can be systematically modified while overall alloy composition is held constant.
Increasing the BCC phase fraction will produce stronger FCC/BCC interfaces.
Increasing the BCC phase fraction or improving the interfaces will reduce the creep strain rate relative to the baseline coating.
Increasing the BCC phase fraction or improving the interfaces will increase creep rupture life relative to the baseline coating.
The baseline is an as-fabricated FCC/BCC coating with a lower BCC volume fraction and unoptimized interphase properties.
The proposed effect operates under sustained high-temperature stress sufficient to activate creep but below catastrophic plastic flow or phase instability.
Thermally stable microstructures can contribute to high-temperature creep resistance in high-entropy alloys.
Defect-related strengthening associated with low matrix stacking-fault energy and high precipitate anti-phase-boundary energy can contribute to high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
The quantitative effect of BCC content and FCC/BCC interface tailoring on creep remains undetermined.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction or rupture-life improvement after increasing BCC content or engineering the interfaces would falsify the hypothesis.
